cards.source_text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war. For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address. Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”. Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.” On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”. But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered. For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage. For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn. For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. cards.source_text: Eight killed and others missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus - Published At least eight people have died and more than a dozen others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said. Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus, said the ferry had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia. The ship's captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation into "how this tragedy occurred", Üstel wrote on social media. A search and rescue operation to find the passengers still unaccounted for is under way, which Turkish authorities have joined. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT). Üstel said the boat had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday, but had been delayed due to poor weather conditions. He told Turkish media outlet TRT that the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he told the outlet. Helicopters and coastguard boats have been dispatched to the scene, while ambulances have been stationed on the beach ready to receive rescued passengers. Üstel wrote on social media that the "priority right now is human life", adding that security forces, rescue teams and health officials were all on the scene. He added the disaster will be thoroughly investigated and "even the slightest negligence will be uncovered". "No one will be spared, regardless of who they are, who is found to be at fault or responsible," Üstel said. Erhan Arikli, the transport minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media that 100 passengers had been taken to shore. Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sent his condolences to Turkish Cypriots and said efforts to reach those who were still missing "continue uninterrupted". "Immediately after the accident, we launched extensive search-and-rescue operations in co-operation with the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus," he said at a military ceremony on Sunday. Mustafa Koc saved around 65 people with his boat after the vessel capsized. He told the BBC that he felt the crew should have waited until the sea was calm. "

cards.source_text: US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island in first known attack in weeks - Published US forces have struck two Iranian launchers on Iran's Larak island, a US official said, marking the first known American strikes on Iran since late July. "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into Strait of Hormuz," the BBC's US partner CBS News quoted US Central Command spokesman Cdr Tim Hawkins as saying. The IRGC said the attack on Sunday killed and wounded several people, and vowed "response and punishment". It marks the first known US strike in Iran since US President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July. The US said it had finished clearing all mines from the strait's main shipping lane earlier this month. - How the US could try to seize Iran's Kharg Island - Published30 March - US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told - Published2 days ago - Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions - Published5 days ago Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping. Iran is currently making tanker traffic pass by this island for checking and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (£1.5m) to cross. Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC's spokesman called the attack a "strategic and fatal mistake by the Trump regime" and said that the "enemy will pay the consequences of this miscalculation in both the economic and military fields". Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack was carried out by drones. Reports indicate that two people were killed and two others injured, it said. Trump said last week that all mines placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship or boat deploying new mines would be destroyed. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump's claim as a "propaganda" deception. Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies. Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict. cards.source_text: US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month, a US official said Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the US attack on Larak island killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to punish those responsible. US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month on Sunday, according to a US official, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military movements. The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes. Semiofficial news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.” The statement said the attack will “result in punishment of the aggressor.” The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran. The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe. He stressed last week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes. Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home. cards.context: 苏丹武装部队与快速支援部队自2026年初爆发冲突，战火蔓延至乡村，迫使平民逃离家园，涌向相对安全的城市。
cards.source_analysis: 报道来自《卫报》，该报以社会公正报道著称，立场偏自由派，关注弱势群体和人道危机。
cards.social_impact: 奥贝德市收容难民数量远超承载能力，食物、水、医疗等基本物资短缺，儿童营养不良风险高，亟需国际援助。
cards.source_text: Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside. The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children. “The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety. The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.” The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago. While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August. “During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.” Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict. Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine. Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege. cards.source_title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city

cards.source_text: DOHA, August 31. /TASS/. Explosions were heard in the south and east of Jordan following Iranian missile strikes, the Fars news agency reported citing Arab sources. Meanwhile, Fox News journalist Trey Yingst wrote on the X social network, citing a US source that "Iran is attacking US forces stationed in Jordan." In his words, nearly all incoming missiles have been intercepted, causing no significant impact. No other details are known at this point. Earlier, Axios and Israel’s Channel 12 correspondent Barak Ravid said that US forces had struck two missile launchers on the island of Larak in southern Iran.

cards.source_text: MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Countries of the Persian Gulf have not imposed any restrictions on air traffic in the region amid reports of Iran’s missile attack on US ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a source in a Middle Eastern air traffic service has told TASS. "No information from Persian Gulf air traffic controllers regarding any restrictions in their respective airspaces has been received," the source said. Earlier in the day, the Islamic Republic’s Press TV television reported that the armed forces of Iran have fired missiles towards US ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Prior to that, Axios and Israel’s Channel 12 correspondent Barak Ravid said on Sunday that US forces had struck two missile launchers on the island of Larak in southern Iran.
cards.source_title: No restrictions on air traffic in Gulf countries imposed — air traffic controllers

cards.source_text: MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. NATO’s military activities in the Extreme North raise risks of incidents with catastrophic consequences, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in his article, ‘International Cooperation in the Arctic: Challenges and Opportunities,’ published on the arctic.ru portal. In the minister’s words, persevering the Arctic region as a zone of peace and cooperation reflects interests of the entire global community, and Russia certainly shares this opinion. However, "there are those who do not share this point of view." "How else can one explain the fact that NATO countries, as well as the Alliance as a whole, are driving the region towards militarisation and creating hotbeds of international tension there?" Lavrov asked rhetorically. In his words, NATO launched Operation Arctic Sentry in February 2026, aimed at expanding its military presence in the High North. "Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries and introducing new components of its command-and-control system," the top Russian diplomat wrote. "Such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security. It also increases the risk of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences."
cards.source_title: NATO military activities in Arctic may lead to catastrophic consequences — Lavrov

cards.source_text: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism. Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel. Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”. The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid. The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt. Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers. “There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect. Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos. But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.” Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March
cards.source_title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’

cards.relevant: 野生动物走私是全球性犯罪，威胁生物多样性，此案显示南非在打击此类非法贸易方面的执法行动。

cards.source_text: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking. A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement. The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species. Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment. South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants. The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.” Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added. The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units. South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.
cards.source_title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs

cards.relevant: 这起案件涉及珍贵文化遗产的流失，且是欧洲博物馆连环抢劫潮的一部分，引发对文物安保和跨国文物走私的关注。

cards.source_analysis: 卫报是英国左翼主流媒体，报道通常详实，对文化事件有持续关注，立场相对中立。
cards.social_impact: 被盗项链价值连城，且具有历史意义，事件引发公众对博物馆安全措施和文物保护的讨论，可能推动相关机构加强安保。
cards.source_text: Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty. Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions. The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace. In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.” Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang. MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time. Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m. The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection. A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed. European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m. In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards. This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina. T
cards.source_title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid

cards.title: 冰岛公投否决重启欧盟入盟谈判

cards.summary: 据冰岛国家广播公司RUV报道，冰岛公投结果显示，52.8%的选民反对政府重启欧盟入盟谈判的提议。此次公投投票率创近二十年新高，反映了冰岛社会对欧盟成员国身份问题的深刻分歧。
cards.relevant: 冰岛是欧洲经济区成员，但非欧盟成员国，此次公投结果将影响其未来与欧盟的关系及外交政策走向。
cards.context: 冰岛曾于2009年申请加入欧盟，但谈判在2013年搁置。此次政府提议重启谈判，但选民通过公投表达了反对意见。
cards.source_analysis: BBC是英国公共广播机构，报道通常客观中立，引用冰岛官方媒体数据，可信度较高。
cards.social_impact: 公投的高投票率显示冰岛民众对欧盟议题的高度关注，结果可能加剧国内政治辩论，并影响冰岛与欧盟的经济合作。
cards.source_text: Iceland votes against restarting EU membership talks - Published Iceland has voted against resuming talks on joining the European Union 13 years after they were broken off. Public broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of the more than 225,000 people who voted had rejected the government's proposal, while 47.2% had backed it. Some 12,600 votes separated them. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland. However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns. With some 270,000 people eligible to vote, RUV reported the turnout of 82.5% was the highest in any Icelandic election since 2009. Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, full EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the eurozone currency union. Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system. Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put those talks on hold. Fishing rights were the biggest obstacle to Icelandic accession then - as they remain today. Iceland fought successfully to protect its fisheries from foreign fishermen during the Cod Wars with the UK in the 1970s - shortly after gaining independence from Denmark - and the country's fish and marine industries still account for almost 40% of its exports. Many No voters feared EU membership would mean ceding some control of these lucrative fishing grounds under the bloc's policies, which control how much a member state can catch. "The No side was much more skillful in sort of tapping into the political national identity in Iceland, which emphasises formal independence, coming out of a long independence struggle coming out of Denmark," Eirikur Bergmann, a professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC. "And so they were able to appeal to people's very fundamental feelings." On the other hand, the Yes campaign "ran an overtly technical campaign, never really explaining the purpose or the passion in why Iceland join the EU", he said. cards.source_text: Manhunt after shooting at Swiss rave kills woman, 22, and injures five - Published A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting at a rave in Switzerland. Italian national Maria Spinelli died at the scene in Aarau on Sunday morning, police said. Four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe". Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible". Aarau cantonal police spokesman Michael Leupold told a news conference on Sunday afternoon that officers were "still in the midst of the operation" and had no leads on who may have been behind the shooting. Organisers and performers said the shooting happened at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in the town, which is located some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich. The force said it had received an initial report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at around 02:30 local time (00:30 GMT). Leupold reiterated that the police were conducting a large-scale, nationwide manhunt for the perpetrator, but said that there were currently no leads on whether it was one person or multiple individuals. They were not believed to be in Aarau anymore, he added. The investigation is being carried out in co-operation with Freiburg police, German news agency DPA reported. Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation". It added that two other Italians "were slightly injured and have already returned home". The Italian Embassy in Bern and the Consulate in Zurich were monitoring the situation, they said. A DJ, who was due to perform until the scheduled end of the event at 02:00, said the incident occurred "straight after our set", in a post on social media. Another performer, DJ Tekibo, said he had lost a friend in the incident. He wrote on Instagram that he was "still trying to process what happened". Olivier Grein, whose firm Agency Events AG organised the event, said the company was "shaken" and would do all it could to support the police investigation. An eyewitness told Blick that he "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped at 02:30, initially believing they were fireworks. He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was then shot. Organisers had expected up to 3,500 people to attend. Police
